title: Rabbi Avichai Rontzki, of Blessed Memory
content:
Rabbi Avichai Rontzki, of Blessed Memory
Rabbi Avichai Rontzki (1951–2018) was one of the most central and complex figures in modern religious Zionism, whose work embodied a rare synthesis of combat military leadership, Torah-halakhic leadership and settlement activity. The present report aims to present comprehensively and in depth his biographical path, the principles of his Torah teaching, and the influence of his rulings and reforms on the army and on Israeli society.
Part One: The Path of the Warrior and the Leader: Biography and the Shaping of His Character
1.1. Biographical Background and the Ideological Transformation
Rabbi Rontzki, also known as "Avi" [1, 2], was born in 1951 (14 Tishrei 5712).[1] He began his path as a classic military man, educated at a military boarding school, and served as a combat soldier and as an officer of high command rank. He served in the Paratroopers and commanded a company in the Shaked reconnaissance unit during the Yom Kippur War.[1] His early combat service was not merely a biographical chapter but a formative event that deeply influenced his future teaching.
After the war, Rontzki described a sense of a breakdown of values. He testified that the values of comradeship, love of the homeland and dedication to the mission, as he had known them from secular military education, had "cracked."[1] His inner feeling was that he was merely quoting slogans that were not "entirely true."[1] This analysis suggests that the experience of the erosion of values after the Yom Kippur War served as the central factor that directly linked his military past with his turn to a life of Torah and ideology. The search for a firm foundation of values, capable of supplying the "fighting spirit" needed by the people of Israel [1], led him to the conclusion that only a Zionism connected to the roots of the Torah and the Land can provide a true answer.
1.2. Torah Study, Settlement and the Founding of Institutions
After his turn to the world of Torah, Rabbi Rontzki joined the educational institutions of the stream of the "yeshivot of the line" (yeshivot ha-kav), which combines intensive Torah study with significant military service and an ideological commitment to settlement. He was a partner in founding the Elon Moreh yeshiva in 1980 and taught there as a ram (yeshiva lecturer), and he also served as a ram at the Ateret Cohanim yeshiva in Jerusalem.[3]
Rabbi Rontzki was a key figure in the settlement movement in Judea and Samaria. In 1984 he was among the founders of the settlement of Itamar [3] and served as the settlement's rabbi in its first years. In 1998 he founded the higher yeshiva in Itamar, which numbered about 190 students, married scholars (avrechim) and staff members.[3, 4] His combined activity in settlement and in the world of Torah cannot be separated from his teaching on "taking responsibility for the systems of the state" [3], since in his eyes settlement was perceived as a practical application of Torah-national sovereignty. He retired from the headship of the yeshiva in Sivan 5776.[4]
The personal journey and public responsibility: A central event attesting to Rabbi Rontzki's consistency between teaching and practice took place in the year 5776 (2016). He volunteered to donate a kidney to whoever might need one through the "Matnat Chaim" (Gift of Life) organization.[4] In the preliminary medical tests for the transplant operation a cancerous tumor was discovered in him, which led to surgery to remove it.[4] He died on 16 Nisan 5778 (2018), after a struggle with the illness, leaving behind a wife and six children.[4] His readiness for dramatic personal sacrifice, in the realm of health as well, expresses a deep consistency with his demand of others for deep involvement and responsibility for the sake of the community.
1.3. His Tenure as Chief Military Rabbi
In 2006 (5766), Rabbi Rontzki was promoted to the rank of Brigadier General and appointed the fifth Chief Military Rabbi of the IDF, a post in which he served until 2010.[1, 4] He entered the post at a sensitive moment in internal military and political terms, after the trauma of the Disengagement, in which the Military Rabbinate stood at the center of a storm. His background as a senior combat officer on the one hand, and as an ideological man of settlement on the other, enabled him to bridge these gaps. He succeeded in stabilizing the Rabbinate's relations with the senior command echelon thanks to his military language and operational experience, and at the same time preserved trust among the public of the settlers and the yeshivot.
Part Two: The Foundations of His Torah and Ideological Teaching: Torah, Army and National Commitment
Rabbi Rontzki's teaching was anchored in an integrative conception, which saw the army as an indispensable instrument for realizing the national-religious destiny, and the Torah as the source of energy for victory.
2.1. The Principle of State Responsibility and the Doctrine of "the Rabbi as Commander"
Rabbi Rontzki's central educational and ideological method called for **"taking responsibility for the Torah and for the systems of the state"** [3], such as the education system and the army.[3] This conception rejected the model of separatism or the model of providing religious services alone, and demanded active involvement in establishing and running state sovereignty.
This conception was illustrated by the abolition of the traditional functional separation between rabbi and commander. Rontzki determined: "There is no difference between a military rabbi and a commander. The role of the military rabbi is exactly the same role as that of the commander: to strengthen the spirit of the soldiers."[1] He did not content himself with a theoretical statement but applied it in practice, as he described his entry into Gaza: "I sat in the commander's jeep... to strengthen the soldiers and to be with them."[1]
This integrative model of leadership gave the Military Rabbinate a practical and command mandate, beyond the traditional roles of kashrut and religion. In this way Rabbi Rontzki posed a challenge both to the secular approach, which sees the rabbi as a passive figure providing a service, and to more conservative rabbinic conceptions, which demanded that the military rabbi maintain absolute neutrality in matters of command or education. The rabbi's role was defined as a strengthener of spirit, whose presence in the field is a condition for carrying out the value-driven mission.
2.2. The Theology of the Fighting Spirit: Zionism as a Conquering Force
At the basis of Rontzki's teaching stood the identification of the true source of victory in war. He rejected the exclusivity of technology, mathematics or physics as decisive factors. In his view, "What wins is the fighting spirit. It is Zionism. It is the connection to the Land."[1] These words were said as part of a sharp critique of secular educational institutions, which in his view had neglected the teaching of love of the Land and of the values of Zionism and had allowed an "economic discourse" to take over, which caused a decline in motivation for combat service.[1]
The insistence on ideology as an operational need turned the cultivation of the fighting spirit into a strategic matter. If the spirit is the winning weapon, then the Military Rabbinate, which is charged with strengthening the spirit by means of "Jewish Consciousness," becomes an operational-strategic unit. This is the theological premise that enabled him to expand the authority of the Rabbinate into the areas of education and values in a significant way.
2.3. The Doctrine of Military Halakha: The "Ke-Chitzim be-Yad Gibor" Series
Rabbi Rontzki's central halakhic enterprise is the book series "Ke-Chitzim be-Yad Gibor" ("As Arrows in the Hand of a Mighty Man"), which comprises four parts and constitutes a collection of halakhic questions and answers concerning matters of army and war.[2, 3] This series, composed by a rabbi with deep operational command experience, expresses the attempt to establish a modern halakhic code out of "his involvement in and acquaintance with army life."[4]
The books reflect a practical approach to halakhic ruling, focused on providing operational solutions, and combine Torah principles with the changing demands of the field. This is an attempt to build a stable halakhic bridge between the world of the beit midrash and the world of the army, in which combat reality dictates the priorities.
Part Three: Expanding the Boundaries of Authority: The Military Rabbinate and the Ideological Reforms
During his tenure as Chief Military Rabbi, Rabbi Rontzki advanced two central reforms that redefined the status and role of the Military Rabbinate, while creating internal and external tensions.
3.1. The "Jewish Consciousness" Reform and the Institutional Confrontation
Rabbi Rontzki placed strong emphasis on expanding the scope of activity of the "Jewish Consciousness" (Jewish Consciousness) field, which had previously been called "Torah Values for Combat."[3, 4, 5] The expansion of the Rabbinate's mandate into the value-educational-national sphere was perceived as essential to strengthening the fighting spirit, as his teaching required.[3] He even argued that a personal meeting of a rabbi with seven soldiers at an outpost, speaking with them about current affairs, is more effective than "study days of the kind where there are 300 soldiers and suddenly some magician arrives" [1], thereby emphasizing the importance of personal interaction and of conveying the value message.
This activity of the Military Rabbinate drew significant criticism from many quarters within the army and outside it. The central claim was that the Rabbinate was "invading the domain of the Education Corps" [3], and thereby undermining the institutional balance in the IDF.
Regulating the field and analyzing the dilemma: The tension reached its peak after Operation Cast Lead, in which members of the Rabbinate accompanied the forces in the field. Following the operation, the then Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Gabi Ashkenazi, held a meeting with the Chief Education Officer and with Rabbi Rontzki, with the aim of "regulating the division of roles between the two bodies."[3] The Chief of Staff did thank the Rabbinate for "strengthening the fighting spirit," but he also criticized members of the Rabbinate who had distributed a booklet "that has a political tinge."[3]
This case illustrates the central dilemma of his tenure: how can one instill a religious-national ideology, which in his eyes is needed to strengthen the spirit of the fighters, in a state army without crossing the line that separates values from a partisan political position. The command recognition of the necessity of strengthening the spirit on the one hand, and the limits that were set on the other, created a constant tension around the boundaries of the Rabbinate's authority.
3.2. Refusal of Orders: The Preference for State Obedience
The issue of refusing orders, which was especially charged after the Disengagement, put Rabbi Rontzki to a test of halakhic and public leadership vis-à-vis parts of the religious-national public. Throughout his tenure he spoke out firmly against ideological refusal of orders.[3]
Position and halakhic reasoning: His position was clear: "It does not matter what my private position is, but if the state decides to evacuate a place, the army must carry out the order."[3] He made clear that this duty applies to "every place."[3] When he was asked to respond to the ruling of Rabbi Avraham Shapira, who called for refusing orders, Rabbi Rontzki rejected his words and replied that "it makes no difference, because the great majority of the rabbis in the religious public ruled that one must not refuse orders."[3]
This position, which set the principle of "taking responsibility" for the systems of the state as a halakhic duty requiring full institutional obedience to the elected government and to the army, strengthened his standing as a statist Chief Military Rabbi. He served as an anchor of halakhic stability, and thereby prevented a more comprehensive rabbinic undermining of the army from within, while upholding the command and state hierarchy.
Part Four: Distinctive Halakhic Issues and Public Controversies
4.1. Expanding the Boundaries of Pikuach Nefesh: The Presence of the Military Rabbi on Shabbat
One of the sharpest halakhic controversies surrounding Rabbi Rontzki concerned his broad interpretation of the concept of pikuach nefesh (saving life) in the context of the fighting spirit. The controversy arose on the eve of Passover that fell on Shabbat in 5768 (19 April 2008), when Rabbi Rontzki joined commanders who had been rushed to the Gaza Strip following an infiltration by terrorists.[3] Conservative rabbis criticized him sharply, arguing that his joining had not been directly necessary in operational terms and therefore constituted an unnecessary desecration of Shabbat.[3]
The original halakhic justification (a letter): In response, Rabbi Rontzki presented a complex halakhic argument. He claimed that the role of the military rabbi derives from the figure of the priest anointed for war, who stands before the fighters, "instills in them a fighting spirit, and subsequently – even goes out with them to the battlefield."[3]
His central halakhic innovation was based on expanding the boundaries of pikuach nefesh: he compared the strengthening of the fighting spirit to the situation of "a dangerously ill person."[3] According to him, in such a situation the decisors permitted bringing the sick person's relatives (even by means of labors forbidden by the Torah itself) if this improves his state of health. From this Rabbi Rontzki concluded that strengthening the spirit is in effect "vital treatment for saving life."[3] He summed up that "the rabbi is an inseparable part of his unit and goes out with the fighters on their missions even on Shabbat," and that he must carry a cell phone with him at all times in order to be reachable.[3]
This ruling is a consistent application of his conception that the fighting spirit is the factor that wins and saves lives.[1] In this way he turned morale, which is a psychological factor, into a halakhic factor of critical weight that justifies setting aside Shabbat.
4.2. The "Bamahane" Controversy and the Issue of Homosexuals
A further public controversy arose in July 2009, following the publication in the weekly "Bamahane" of an interview with a religious homosexual officer. Rabbi Rontzki sent a sharply worded letter to the head of the Manpower Directorate and to the Chief Education Officer.[3]
His explicit position was that "there is no place for an article about people with inverted inclinations in the army's newspaper."[3] This position drew public condemnation, but it reflects his conception that the army is not a neutral body in terms of social values, but is obliged to preserve a religious-traditional framework of values that promotes certain norms. Any deviation from this was perceived in his eyes as harming the "spirit" required for victory, and the value foundation required of the army.

Part Five: Summary and Legacy: Rabbi Rontzki's Influence on Religious Zionism and the IDF
The legacy of Rabbi Avichai Rontzki lies in his halakhic and practical bridging between worlds that were considered opposed: the combat world of the operational officer corps, and the ideological world of the settlement yeshivot.
5.1. Instilling the Doctrine of Involvement and Subordinating Halakha to the Operational Need
Rabbi Rontzki turned the ideology of "taking responsibility for the systems of the state" into a practical program of work. This approach was a central driving factor that led to the integration and advancement of graduates of the yeshivot of the line in the senior ranks of the army, while he supplied them with the theoretical and halakhic foundation that made this possible. His teaching pushed the religious-national public to turn from a peripheral force into a dominant and leading force in the combat command.
The "Ke-Chitzim be-Yad Gibor" book series is the theoretical foundation of his rulings, constituting a binding and up-to-date halakhic tool. By means of these books and of the reforms in the Military Rabbinate, Rontzki redefined the role of the military rabbi as a command factor with a value-driven mission, his mission to strengthen the fighting spirit being in every respect a mission of pikuach nefesh.
5.2. The Complexity of His Figure and His Place in the National-Religious Discourse
The figure of Rabbi Rontzki represents a unique duality: an ideological leader from the world of ostensibly extreme settlement who became a committed statist leader. He succeeded in maintaining a fine balance: he dramatically strengthened the connection between Jewish identity and military functioning (by means of "Jewish Consciousness"), but at the same time he firmly defended the cohesion of the army and the principle of state obedience through his position against refusing orders. This statist position, which involved an internal confrontation with rabbis within his own public, enabled him to preserve the continuity of the army's functioning and to prevent the undermining of its authority.
In essence, Rabbi Rontzki acted as the builder of a two-way bridge: he brought active religious Zionism into the army, and at the same time brought the operational language and state commitment into the world of the yeshivot. His legacy is not merely a collection of rulings, but a complete model of life demonstrating how halakha, Zionism and military command can combine to create an ideology that accepts full responsibility for the fate of the nation and the state.
